title: Managing laying hens through a severe winter
subtitle: Keeping a small flock laying and healthy when temperatures drop hard.
excerpt: Laying hens drop egg production significantly below five degrees and can suffer frostbite on large combs and wattles during prolonged cold snaps. Good winter management comes down to: a draught-free but ventilated coop, unfrozen water available at all times, enough calories in the feed to cover the energy cost of keeping warm, and knowing which breeds tolerate cold better than others.
sourceNotes: DEFRA Code of Recommendations for the Welfare of Laying Hens (2018). Gail Damerow, Storey's Guide to Raising Chickens (2017), chapter on winter management. University of Kentucky Extension, Winter Poultry Management (2021). Lewis Wright, The Practical Poultry Keeper (1867), Internet Archive.

glossaryTerms.definition: Damage to the comb, wattles, or feet of a chicken caused by ice crystal formation in the tissue during prolonged exposure to sub-zero temperatures. Affected tissue appears pale then black; small blisters may develop.

The annual shedding and replacement of feathers in poultry, typically triggered by shortening day length in late summer or autumn. Hens stop laying during the moult and resume after regrowing feathers.

content.text: Laying hens slow their egg production and can suffer welfare problems when temperatures fall hard and stay low. The core risks in a severe winter are: frozen water supplies, frostbite on exposed combs and wattles, and a calorie deficit if hens are burning more energy keeping warm than the ration provides. None of these is difficult to manage with a bit of foresight.
The coop in winter

A winter coop needs to be draught-free at roost height without being poorly ventilated. These two things sound contradictory but are not: draughts at bird level are cold air moving directly across roosting birds, stripping warmth. Ventilation is moist warm air from respiration and droppings escaping through a ridge gap or high vents, to be replaced by fresh cool air from lower inlets. A damp, poorly ventilated coop with condensation on the walls is a worse environment than a cool, dry, well-ventilated one.
Block any gaps at roost height that are not intended ventilation: gaps in the walls below the top board, cracks around the pop-hole, damaged fascia boards.
Ensure the high ventilation (ridge vent or board gap near the roof apex) remains open: moisture must escape.
Add extra bedding on the coop floor: a deep-litter system with 15 cm of wood shavings generates some heat from decomposition and keeps feet warm.
Water in a freeze
Hens will not eat properly if they cannot drink freely: feed and water are closely linked in a hen's digestion. Check water at least twice a day in sub-zero weather. Options for preventing freezing:
Keep a second drinker indoors, rotating the frozen one with a warm one each morning and evening.
Sit the drinker on a flat stone slab in a sunny spot: the stone absorbs heat and delays freezing.
A thermostat-controlled poultry drinker heater pad is reliable in prolonged hard frost.
Feeding in cold weather

Hens burn more calories in cold weather staying warm. Do not reduce the feed ration in winter: if anything, increase it slightly and add a handful of whole wheat or barley in the afternoon. Whole grain takes longer to digest than pellets and generates a little more metabolic heat overnight as it breaks down in the gizzard.
Frostbite on combs and wattles
Large-combed breeds (Leghorn, Spanish, Minorca) are at higher risk of
frostbite on the comb
than rose-combed breeds (Wyandotte, Dorking, Silkie). In areas with regular hard frosts, choose rose-combed varieties.

Petroleum jelly (Vaseline) applied to combs and wattles on nights forecast below minus five degrees provides a degree of protection by reducing ice crystal formation on the surface. It is not a guaranteed prevention in prolonged hard frost but it helps.

Frostbitten tissue on a comb appears pale then black as the frost damage progresses. Small areas of tip frostbite rarely cause serious welfare problems. A fully frostbitten comb that is blackening at the base needs veterinary attention.
Egg production expectations
A hen that has
moulting

in autumn will resume laying in December or January once the new feathers are fully in. A hen that did not moult heavily may continue laying at a reduced rate through the winter. Do not use supplemental lighting to force winter laying if you want hens to lay productively for several years: a hen that lays year-round at 18 hours of light runs through her finite egg supply faster and retires earlier.

attrs.cue: Hens refuse to leave the coop in cold weather
attrs.cause: Snow or frost on the ground; discomfort from walking on cold surfaces
attrs.fix: Lay a path of straw or wood shavings from the pop-hole to the feeder and drinker. Hens will use it. Do not force hens out in snow: access to outdoor range is a welfare benefit, not a welfare requirement in harsh conditions.

attrs.cue: Eggs are freezing inside the coop overnight
attrs.cause: Coop too cold; eggs not collected before dark
attrs.fix: Collect eggs at dusk when hens go to roost, before overnight temperatures fall. A frozen egg with a cracked shell should be discarded.
